big: A stranger on a messaging group says: 'Put in ₹50,000 and get ₹1 lakh in a month, guaranteed.' Thousands of people have lost money to this one sentence, in many different costumes.

lines: The group has hundreds of members, and people post their profits. It must be real?
Profit screenshots are very easy to fake. Look for the shared warning signs instead of the story.

title: Red flags
stops: No genuine investment can guarantee high returns
A big group of members proves a scheme is safe
Pressure to decide today is a warning sign
An adviser needs no registration to charge fees
caps: Markets rise and fall, so a promise of fixed high profit with no risk is false.
Crowds and screenshots are easy to fake, so they prove nothing.
Scammers rush you so that you do not have time to check.
Paid advice needs a registration, which you can verify.

intro: What the promise would really mean.
note: No bank, fund or business earns this. A promise like it is not an opportunity. It is the warning sign.

q: A caller says Meena's money will double in a month, with no risk. What does this most likely show?
opts: A warning sign of a scam
A special offer for smart investors
A deal that banks cannot match yet
A government scheme with rare access
why: No genuine investment can promise high profit with no risk, so this is a red flag.
Real investors check claims. A promise this large is not a mark of smartness.
Banks cannot match it because no honest product can make such a promise.
Government schemes do not promise doubled money in a month, to anyone.

q: A message says: 'Join in the next hour or lose your place.' What should Rohan do?
opts: Pay quickly to secure the place
Send the link on to his friends
Slow down, since rushing is a trick
Share his bank details to hold it
why: Paying in a hurry is exactly what the message is built to cause.
Forwarding spreads the risk to his friends and does nothing to verify it.
Urgency is used so that he cannot check, so a pause is the safest step.
Bank details given in haste can be used to take money from him.

q: A social media page sells paid stock tips. Which question matters most before paying?
opts: How many followers does the page have today?
How bright and neat are the page photos?
Did a friend of a friend pay for it?
Is he registered, and can I verify it?
why: Followers can be bought, so the number says little about honesty.
Photos are made to attract and say nothing about the adviser's standing.
A friend's payment is not a check, since friends can be fooled too.
Paid advice needs a registration that can be checked on the regulator's list.

q: Meena sees screenshots of big profits in a group. What is the right view?
opts: They can be faked, proving nothing
They prove that the group is registered
They show that the profit is guaranteed
why: A picture of a profit does not show that the scheme is real or sound.
Screenshots are easy to fake, so they are no evidence at all.
Registration is shown on the regulator's list and not in a chat group.
No screenshot can show a guarantee, since no guarantee can be real.

pts: Guaranteed high returns are a lie, since every investment carries risk.
Pressure to hurry is a trick to stop you checking.
Paid advice needs a registration. Screenshots and crowds prove nothing.
